KEY WebACL CONFIG FACTS (important for interpreting "got through"):
- DefaultAction = ALLOW. Requests that match only COUNT rules (or no rule) are ALLOWED and reach the origin.
- In the AWS-AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet, the sub-rules `CrossSiteScripting_QUERYARGUMENTS` and `CrossSiteScripting_BODY` are OVERRIDDEN TO COUNT — so XSS in query args or body is NOT blocked, only counted; those requests reach the origin. This is a prime "got through" vector.
- Other COUNT-only rules whose matches still reach origin: custom-geo-block-antarctica (country AQ), custom-sensitive-uri-rate (/admin, 60/5min), BotControl SignalNonBrowserUserAgent and CategoryHttpLibrary.
- SQLi ruleset and KnownBadInputs block by default. A SQLi/exploit variant that EVADED those managed rules would appear as ALLOW with no corresponding block label — so also inspect ALLOW payloads directly.

- Database: `waf_analysis_tmp`, Table: `waf_logs_response_id_on_page`, Athena WorkGroup: `devops-agent`.

- Partition `log_time` STRING 'yyyy/MM/dd/HH/mm'. ALWAYS filter, e.g. WHERE log_time >= '2026/09/08/03/00' AND log_time <= '2026/09/08/04/30'.

- Nested (Trino): `httprequest` struct(clientip,country,uri,args,httpmethod,host,requestid,headers:array<struct<name,value>>). `labels` array<struct<name>> — contains WAF labels such as 'awswaf:managed:aws:core-rule-set:CrossSiteScripting_QueryArguments', SQLi labels, bot labels. `nonterminatingmatchingrules` array<struct<ruleid,action,rulematchdetails:array<struct<conditiontype,sensitivitylevel,location,matcheddata:array<string>>>>> — COUNT matches on an ALLOWED request appear here. Use CROSS JOIN UNNEST to flatten labels / nonterminatingmatchingrules.

YOUR TASKS (incident window 03:00–04:30, focus on action='ALLOW' = 4585 requests):
1. Correlate by attacker IP: first identify the set of clientips that were BLOCKED in the window (SELECT DISTINCT httprequest.clientip ... WHERE action='BLOCK'). Then count how many ALLOW requests in the window came FROM those same clientips, and sample them. These are requests from known-malicious actors that WERE allowed through — inspect their uri/args/httpmethod for attack payloads.
2. XSS-that-got-through: find ALLOW requests whose `labels` include any CrossSiteScripting label, OR whose `nonterminatingmatchingrules` include a CrossSiteScripting ruleid (because XSS query-args/body is Count-only here). 3. Any other COUNT-only matches on ALLOW requests (geo AQ, /admin sensitive-uri-rate, SQLi labels present but action=ALLOW, bot labels): enumerate via labels / nonterminatingmatchingrules and report counts + samples. Report any matches with the clientip, uri, args, and whether that same clientip was also in the blocked set.
5. For any suspicious ALLOW requests found, report `responsecodesent` if present, and note the host and requestid so impact can be traced.

Your sole focus: determine, with evidence, whether any malicious/attack traffic was ALLOWED through to the origin, how much, from whom, and of what type.

# Findings — WAF Attack Payload Characterization (BLOCKED requests)

**Scope:** CloudFront WebACL `response-id-on-page`, host `website.a.example.com`, account 012345678901_1 / us-east-1. Incident window 2026-09-08 03:00:00Z–04:30:00Z, `action='BLOCK'` only. (Timeline/IP-geo attribution and ALLOW-traffic analysis excluded per scope.)

## Sub-rule breakdown (which rules fired and where)

| Managed rule set | Sub-rule (ruleid) | conditiontype | location | Blocks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AWS-AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet | `SQLi_QUERYARGUMENTS` | SQL_INJECTION | **ALL_QUERY_ARGS** | **122** |
| AWS-AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet | `ExploitablePaths_URIPATH` | REGEX | **URI** | **10** |

- **100% of SQLi blocks** matched on the query string (`ALL_QUERY_ARGS` / QUERY_STRING) — none on BODY, COOKIE, HEADER, or URI path. All were `GET` requests.
- **100% of KnownBadInputs blocks** matched on the URI path via regex. No matcheddata is populated (the signature is the path itself, `/.env`), and `args` was empty.

## Task 1 — SQLi (122 blocks): techniques & verbatim payloads

Matched data confirmed from `terminatingrulematchdetails` (verbatim tokens WAF flagged). The 122 blocks decompose into **12 canonical payloads repeated 10× each (120)** + **2 natural-language false-positives (2)**:

| URI | param | Payload (URL-decoded) | matcheddata tokens | Technique | Count |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| /search | `q` | `' OR '1'='1` | `[, OR, 1, =, 1]` | Boolean tautology (auth/filter bypass) | 10 |
| /login | `id` | `' OR '1'='1` | `[, OR, 1, =, 1]` | Boolean tautology | 10 |
| /search | `q` | `1' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users--` | `[1, UNION, SELECT, username, FROM]` | UNION-based data exfil (credential dump) | 10 |
| /login | `id` | `1' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users--` | `[1, UNION, SELECT, username, FROM]` | UNION-based data exfil | 10 |
| /search | `q` | `1'; EXEC xp_cmdshell('dir')--` | `[1, ;, EXEC, xp_cmdshell, (]` | Stacked query → OS command exec (MSSQL xp_cmdshell) | 10 |
| /login | `id` | `1'; EXEC xp_cmdshell('dir')--` | `[1, ;, EXEC, xp_cmdshell, (]` | Stacked query → OS command exec | 10 |
| /search | `q` | `1; DROP TABLE users;--` | `[1, ;, DROP, TABLE, users]` | Stacked destructive DDL | 10 |
| /login | `id` | `1; DROP TABLE users;--` | `[1, ;, DROP, TABLE, users]` | Stacked destructive DDL | 10 |
| /search | `q` | `1' AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.tables)>0--` | `[1, AND, (, SELECT, COUNT]` | Boolean/schema enumeration (information_schema) | 10 |
| /login | `id` | `1' AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.tables)>0--` | `[1, AND, (, SELECT, COUNT]` | Boolean/schema enumeration | 10 |
| /search | `q` | `admin'--` | — | Comment-evasion auth bypass (comment out password check) | 10 |
| /login | `id` | `admin'--` | — | Comment-evasion auth bypass | 10 |
| /search | `q` | `our UNION workers SELECT new leadership` | — | Natural-language false positive (UNION/SELECT keywords) | 1 |
| /search | `q` | `credit UNION members SELECT best savings plan` | — | Natural-language false positive | 1 |

**SQLi techniques observed (characterization):**
- **Boolean/tautology:** `' OR '1'='1` — classic always-true auth/filter bypass.
- **UNION-based exfiltration:** `UNION SELECT username,password FROM users` — explicit attempt to dump the `users` table credentials.
- **Stacked queries → RCE:** `; EXEC xp_cmdshell('dir')` — MSSQL-specific OS command execution via stacked statement.
- **Stacked destructive DDL:** `; DROP TABLE users;` — data-destruction attempt.
- **Schema enumeration:** `AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.tables)>0` — boolean DB fingerprinting / schema recon.
- **Comment-evasion auth bypass:** `admin'--` — terminates the SQL string and comments out the rest (e.g. password clause).
- **No time-based blind** (no `SLEEP`/`BENCHMARK`/`WAITFOR`) and **no out-of-band** payloads were seen among the blocked traffic.

The payloads form a **uniform, scripted/automated scan**: the exact same 6 payload families fired against both endpoints, each exactly 10 times — strongly indicative of a tool-driven campaign rather than manual probing.

## Task 2 — KnownBadInputs (10 blocks): signatures

- **All 10 blocks** were `GET /.env` (no query args), matched by `ExploitablePaths_URIPATH` (conditiontype `REGEX`, location `URI`).
- **Signature characterization:** This is the **sensitive-file / secrets-disclosure exploit path** signature — attempts to retrieve the application's `.env` file (framework environment/config file commonly leaking DB credentials, API keys, secrets). It is a well-known reconnaissance/exploit probe, **not** Log4j JNDI, path traversal (`../`), or host-header injection — none of those signatures appeared.

## Task 3 — Targeted endpoints & parameters

**Targeted paths (blocked):**
| URI | Rule | Blocks |
|---|---|---|
| `/search` | SQLi | 62 |
| `/login` | SQLi | 60 |
| `/.env` | KnownBadInputs | 10 |

**Targeted parameters (SQLi):**
- `/search` → parameter **`q`**
- `/login` → parameter **`id`**

Both parameters were hit with the identical set of 6 SQLi payload families. `/.env` was targeted directly as a URI path (no parameters).

## Queries run (Athena, DB `waf_analysis_tmp`, WG `devops-agent`)
1. Sub-rule counts via `UNNEST(rulegrouplist)` → `rg.terminatingrule.ruleid` (SQLi_QUERYARGUMENTS=122, ExploitablePaths_URIPATH=10).
2. terminatingruleid counts (SQLiRuleSet=122, KnownBadInputsRuleSet=10).
3. Match details via `UNNEST(terminatingrulematchdetails)` for each rule set — gave conditiontype, location, matcheddata, example requests.
4. Targeted URI counts grouped by terminatingruleid + uri.
5. Full payload distribution: `GROUP BY httprequest.uri, httprequest.args` for SQLi (revealed the 12×10 + 2 structure, including the `admin'--` payload and the 2 natural-language false positives).

Note: the per-managed-rule `rulegrouplist[].terminatingrule.rulematchdetails` arrays were empty; the actionable matcheddata lived in the top-level `terminatingrulematchdetails` array (used for all payload-token evidence above).

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### WAF BLOCK spike: 0 baseline → 132 blocks on response-id-on-page
**Description:** On 2026-09-08 WAF BLOCK volume on the CloudFront WebACL `response-id-on-page` (protecting website.a.example.com) jumped from a flat 0-block baseline (0 blocks in both the prior-day 03:00–04:30 window and the preceding 3 hours) to 132 blocks concentrated in a ~10-minute burst (onset 03:55Z, peak 04:00Z = 115 blocks/87%, tail 04:05Z, quiet by 04:10Z). All 132 blocks were SQLi (122) + KnownBadInputs (10). This is a genuine attack, not elevated background noise.
**Time:** 2026-09-08T03:55:00Z - 2026-09-08T04:05:00Z

### Malicious requests reached origin (not blocked)
**Description:** During the same campaign, multiple categories of attack traffic were ALLOWED through to origin website.a.example.com (all with empty responsecodesent — the origin, not WAF, served the response): 160 reflected-XSS requests, 10 /etc/passwd LFI attempts, 20 recon probes (/actuator/env, /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php), 320 /admin/dashboard probes, plus large-scale /products/{id} catalog enumeration. None carried a SQLi/KnownBadInputs label — so this is 'got through', not 'detected-but-not-blocked'.
**Time:** 2026-09-08T03:19:00Z - 2026-09-08T04:05:00Z

## Findings

### Cause: CRS XSS rules set to Count let XSS reach origin
**Description:** The CommonRuleSet rules `CrossSiteScripting_QUERYARGUMENTS` and `CrossSiteScripting_BODY` are overridden to Count (not Block) in the WebACL. During the incident window, 160 ALLOW requests carried the `awswaf:managed:aws:core-rule-set:CrossSiteScripting_QueryArguments` label — meaning XSS payloads in query arguments were detected but passed through to origin.
**Cascades to:** symptom-got-through

### Cause: No LFI / path-traversal / sensitive-path coverage — recon reached origin
**Description:** The WebACL deploys no Linux/Unix or path-traversal managed rule set, so /etc/passwd (LFI), /actuator/env (Spring Boot info disclosure) and /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php probes matched no blocking rule and were ALLOWED to origin. Additionally, custom-sensitive-uri-rate (/admin, 60/5min) is Count-only, so 320 /admin/dashboard probes passed. These coverage gaps are a cause of malicious traffic reaching origin.
**Cascades to:** symptom-got-through

#### Supporting Observations
- **Exploit-recon paths ALLOWED to origin from attacker IPs:** 65 ALLOW requests came from IPs that were simultaneously blocked for SQLi during the same window. Among the ALLOW traffic are unblocked recon/exploit paths that reached the origin: /etc/passwd (10 requests, LFI/sensitive-file access — all from the blocked attacker IPs), /actuator/env (Spring Boot env/info disclosure), and /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php (WordPress probe). responsecodesent is empty for these (WAF ALLOW passes through to CloudFront/origin). None of these paths are covered by the WebACL's active blocking rules, so they were served by the origin rather than stopped at the edge.

### Root Cause: Single automated actor ran a multi-phase injection + recon campaign
**Description:** The block spike was caused by an external automated attack from a single actor (constant fingerprint JA3 562bacc81ac86e7d4304bb8a98429ddb / JA4 t13d3514h2_bfa337485184_97a66a8f4cb1 / Chrome-125 UA) rotating ~15 AWS/cloud egress IPs across IE/US/SG/IN/JP. Phases, all one campaign: 03:19–03:45 catalog enumeration (/products/{id}) + /admin/dashboard probing; 03:39–03:43 reflected XSS on /search; 03:55–04:05 SQLi on /search?q & /login?id (boolean, UNION cred-exfil, stacked xp_cmdshell RCE, DROP TABLE, information_schema enum, admin'-- bypass); 04:04 /.env + /etc/passwd LFI + actuator/wp-admin recon. The WAF SQLi and KnownBadInputs rule sets fired as designed — the block jump is the WAF working correctly against a real attack. This is the fundamental cause of the observed BLOCK spike.
**Cascades to:** symptom-block-spike, symptom-got-through

## Other Gaps

### Cannot confirm whether exploitation succeeded at origin
**Description:** WAF logs confirm these requests reached origin but cannot confirm whether exploitation succeeded — whether /etc/passwd or /actuator/env returned sensitive content, whether the XSS was reflected, or whether /admin/dashboard exposed data. That requires origin/CloudFront access logs correlated by the request IDs captured during this investigation; those logs were not part of the provided data source. Follow up to confirm actual data exposure.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Harden the CloudFront WAFv2 WebACL `response-id-on-page` to close four coverage gaps that let attack/recon traffic reach origin: (1) enforce the CRS reflected-XSS sub-rules (remove the Count overrides so query-arg and body XSS are Blocked), (2) add the AWS Linux and Unix managed rule sets to block LFI / path-traversal / sensitive-path probes (e.g. /etc/passwd), (3) switch `custom-sensitive-uri-rate` on /admin from Count to Block, (4) retain all existing protections unchanged. Applied as a single atomic update_web_acl with a full-config backup first and a complete rollback path.

## Reasoning
WAF correctly blocked 132 SQLi + /.env requests, but the live config let the same actor through to origin: 160 reflected-XSS (CRS XSS sub-rules overridden to Count), /etc/passwd + /actuator/env + /wp-admin probes (no Linux/Unix managed rule deployed), and 320 /admin/dashboard probes (custom-sensitive-uri-rate set to Count). These are persistent, exploitable misconfigurations — valuable to fix even though the burst subsided. Capacity 1177 WCU leaves ample headroom under the 5000 limit for the two added rule sets. Because origin logs were unavailable, allowed-through traffic is treated as potential exposure, raising priority.
